sections.html:
Charlottesville is an independent city in central Virginia, on the Rivanna River, with Albemarle County all around it. The city and county are separate governments, and only the city bills city addresses. The city covers 10.27 square miles and counted 46,553 residents in 2020.

The University of Virginia shapes the housing market. Its grounds sit mostly in Albemarle County, and more than 20,000 students arrive in the academic year. Older streets near the university, such as Ridge Street, Fifeville, Tenth and Page, and Rose Hill, hold homes with age-related repair needs that buyers will spot quickly.

Real estate tax is due in two equal installments, June 5 and December 5. A deadline that lands on a weekend moves to the following Monday. The city lists a rate of $0.99 per $100 of assessed value, which City Council sets each spring.

Bill detailCity of Charlottesville
Due datesJune 5 and December 5
Rate$0.99 per $100 of assessed value
Late penalty10 percent of the tax due, the day after the deadline
Interest10 percent a year, accruing monthly
Treasurer phone434-970-3146
Mailing addressP.O. Box 2854, Charlottesville, VA 22902

A payment plan does not stop penalties and interest. For unpaid tax, the city lists bank account liens, rent liens and wage garnishments, and properties with three or more years of unpaid tax are subject to judicial sale. To request a penalty waiver, read the city's Late Payment Penalty Policy and write to the Treasurer with supporting documents.

sections.h2: How the City Assessor values property
sections.html:
The City Assessor values every parcel each year as of January 1 and mails change of assessment notices at the end of January. City code calls for annual assessment of all real estate.

Most homes are valued by comparing recent sales of similar houses in the same neighborhood. Auctions, bank foreclosures, condemnations and family transfers generally are not treated as arm's-length sales, which is useful to know if your own house changed hands on unusual terms.

  • Assessor's office: 102 5th Street NE, Charlottesville, VA 22902, by appointment, phone 434-970-3136.
  • Mail: P.O. Box 911, Charlottesville, VA 22902.
  • Commissioner of the Revenue: 605 E Main Street, Room A-130, phone 434-970-3160.

The Assessor keeps a history file on each parcel with ownership, deed and plat references, and details of improvements. The city also posts assessment neighborhood maps, land books and GIS data, and its GIS Viewer opens real estate records online. A public computer at the Assessor's office offers the same access.

  • Neighborhood maps and land books on the city's assessor pages.
  • An Income and Expense form for income-producing property.
  • An Assessment Appeal Application, which you can also request by phone.

Before you list, compare the record with the house. The city takes factual discrepancies such as square footage, acreage or the condition of improvements as grounds for appeal, and a corrected record lowers the bill you hand to the next owner. If an agent files for you, include a Letter of Authorization.

There are three levels: the assessor, the Board of Equalization, then Circuit Court. A high bill or a big jump in value is not enough on its own. The city accepts factual errors in the property record, uneven values within a neighborhood and disagreements over fair market value.

  1. Call the appraiser at 434-970-3136 with your owner name, address or nine-digit parcel ID. Many questions end here.
  2. File an Assessment Appeal Application with your reasoning and evidence. The appraiser may inspect the property and mails a decision, which the city says comes within 30 days.
  3. Ask for a Board of Equalization review within 30 days of the decision letter. The board is an independent citizen panel appointed by the Circuit Court judge, and it mails its decision within 30 days after the hearing.
  4. As a last step, appeal to Circuit Court. You carry the burden of proof and pay court costs.

Call the assessor's office for the filing deadline on the first application. Virginia law, in 58.1-3379, presumes the assessor's value is correct and requires the owner to rebut it with evidence.

The Treasurer's balance includes penalty and interest, so the payoff changes month to month. Ask the Treasurer at 434-970-3146 for a figure that matches your closing date.

The Commissioner of the Revenue lists tax relief programs for older and disabled owners, a homeowner assistance program and an exemption for disabled veterans and surviving spouses. Ask that office which relief programs are open now before you count on one.

At closing, Virginia's grantor tax in 58.1-802 is fifty cents for each $500 of value, normally paid by the seller.

sections.h2: Cash sale for a Charlottesville house
sections.html:
If your house needs repairs or has back tax, Cash Home Buyers can review it as is and plan around the payoff figure from the Treasurer. A cash sale skips the lender appraisal and the repair requests that often come with a financed purchase, which matters most for older homes near the university.

Before any offer, gather your latest assessment notice, your tax bills and receipts, and the payoff figure from the Treasurer. With those in hand, a seller can compare offers on equal terms.

sections.h2: What to bring when you call the city
sections.html: Have the owner name, the street address or the nine-digit parcel ID ready. The assessor, the Treasurer and the Commissioner of the Revenue each keep their own records, so the same details save time with all three. Write down who you spoke with and what they said, especially about penalty waivers or appeal deadlines.

faqs.q: When are Charlottesville real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: June 5 and December 5, in equal installments. A due date that lands on a weekend moves to the next Monday.

faqs.q: What is the Charlottesville real estate tax rate?
faqs.a: The city lists $0.99 per $100 of assessed value, set by City Council each spring. Confirm the current rate with the Treasurer.

faqs.q: How do I dispute my Charlottesville assessment?
faqs.a: Call the City Assessor at 434-970-3136, then file an Assessment Appeal Application. If you disagree with the decision, ask the Board of Equalization to review it within 30 days, and use Circuit Court as the final step.

faqs.q: What happens if Charlottesville property tax goes unpaid?
faqs.a: A 10 percent penalty applies the day after the deadline, and interest accrues at 10 percent a year. The city lists liens and wage garnishment, and judicial sale for three or more years of unpaid tax.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Charlottesville house with tax still due?
faqs.a: Yes, the balance is normally paid from proceeds at closing. Get a current payoff from the Treasurer's Office before the closing date.
